passages.english: …[become liable] to a great charge. "Render," it is written, "the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God." Therefore neither is it permitted to us to rule on earth, nor do you, emperor, have authority to burn incense. These things, then, I write out of concern for your salvation; but concerning the matters about which you wrote, I am of this opinion: I neither agree with the Arians, but on the contrary I anathematize their heresy; nor do I write against Athanasius, whom both we and the church of the Romans and the whole synod cleared. For you yourself, also knowing these things, sent for the man, and allowed him to return with honour to his native land and to the church.
passages.notes: The language is Greek, not Latin: this is the Greek text of Hosius (Ossius) of Cordoba's letter to Constantius preserved by Athanasius. The scan has many errors (? for ς, ρ for μ, etc.), which have been read silently; the numbers (4) and (5) are section marks and are omitted. The passage begins mid-sentence: "ἐγκλήματι μεγάλῳ γένῃ" completes "ὑπεύθυνος" in the preceding context ("lest you become liable to a great charge"). "συνόρων" is taken as a misreading of "συνορῶν" ("perceiving, knowing").
